title: Counting Life
description: Objective: notice everything that is alive around you and begin to work out what it means to be living - breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.
activity: Take ten slow steps, count every living thing you find, then work out together what makes something alive.
preparation: Nothing to bring. Walk out as you are.
space_needed: Any outdoor spot with ten steps of room: a playground corner, a grass edge, a quiet stretch of pavement.

steps.name: Count
steps.note: Set the boundary first: ten steps from where you stand, no further. Pairs work well.

tips.then: Crouch down with them. Grass, moss, a weed in a crack. The small things count.
tips.when: If they say there's nothing here...

tips.then: Ask them to prove each one: what tells you it's alive?
tips.when: If they race to finish first...

tips.then: Count together as one group, pointing as you go.
tips.when: If the counting turns into arguing...

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Count everything that's alive within ten steps.

steps.name: See
steps.note: Encourage children to look up, down, under...

tips.then: Ask for the smallest living thing they can find.
tips.when: If they only name big things...

tips.then: Try a silent minute: point, don't speak.
tips.when: If eyes wander to each other instead...

steps.label: Say to your class

steps.name: Hear
steps.note: Try thirty seconds of complete silence first. The longer the quiet, the more they hear.

tips.then: Cup hands behind ears and wait thirty more seconds. Traffic does not count: what else?
tips.when: If they say they hear nothing...

steps.label: Say to your class

steps.name: Alive
steps.note: Let them argue. A fallen leaf, a seed, moss on a wall: alive or not? The wondering is the learning.

tips.then: Ask: was it alive? Is the tree it came from alive? Both answers teach.
tips.when: If they are unsure about a leaf on the ground...

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: What is telling you it's alive?

steps.name: Living
steps.note: Four signs they can test anything against. Try them on a bird, a tree, a stone.

tips.then: Act them out: breathe in, stretch tall and grow, drift like a seed, flop down.
tips.when: If the words feel too big...

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: What does it mean to be living: breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.

closing_prompts.note: Let a few children share with the whole circle.
closing_prompts.question: What was the most surprising living thing you found?

closing_prompts.note: A feather, a seed, a fallen leaf. Hard cases make the best thinking.
closing_prompts.question: Was anything hard to decide: alive or not alive?

closing_prompts.note: No right answer. Big guesses welcome.
closing_prompts.question: How many living things do you think share our whole school grounds?

primer.why: Naming what is alive is the first step to caring about it. A child who has counted dozens of living things in one corner of the playground never sees "nothing" there again.
primer.summary: Children count everything alive within ten steps of where they stand, then begin to work out what makes something living: breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.

celebration.headline: Your class found life everywhere.
celebration.keepsake: Ten steps. More life than anyone expected.

title: Minibeast Hunting
description: Objective: look closely at minibeasts and discover that all creatures have special roles to help our planet stay alive.
activity: Hunt for minibeasts in soil, under logs and in bushes. Look closely, ask questions, and put every creature back.
preparation: Bring the bug pots or viewers and magnifying glasses. If you can, check your patch the day before: lift a log, see who is home.
space_needed: Soil, a log, a bush or a tree. Any patch where small creatures hide.

steps.name: Engage
steps.note: Allow children to raise their hands to give feedback.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: What minibeasts do you know? Can you name them?
prompts: What minibeasts do you know? Can you name them?
What is your favourite minibeast and why?

steps.name: Explore
steps.note: Give children 10 minutes to explore their outdoor space, using only their senses.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Take 10 minutes to explore. Look under logs, on leaves, in trees, and up in the sky.
prompts: Take 10 minutes to explore. Look under logs, on leaves, in trees, and up in the sky.

steps.name: Identify
steps.note: Bring the class back to the circle. Let them discuss in partners or raise their hands.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: What minibeasts did you find in our grounds?
prompts: What minibeasts did you find in our grounds?
How many legs did they have?
Did they have wings to fly?

steps.name: Appreciate
steps.note: Allow your class to go back to a spot in your grounds to thank the minibeasts.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Go back to a quiet spot and thank a minibeast. They play an important part in keeping our planet alive.
prompts: Go back to a quiet spot and thank a minibeast. They play an important part in keeping our planet alive.

closing_prompts.note: We borrow, we look, we give back. The whole lesson in one move.
closing_prompts.question: Carry your minibeast back to where you found it and say a quiet goodbye.

closing_prompts.note: Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist.
closing_prompts.question: What job was your minibeast doing for our planet?
Which minibeast would you like to be for a day, and why?

primer.why: Minibeasts are the easiest wild animals for children to meet up close. Handling them gently is a first lesson in respect for living things: gentle hands, quiet voices, and everything goes back exactly where it was found.
primer.summary: Children hunt for minibeasts in soil, under logs and in bushes, look closely at legs, wings and homes, and learn that every creature has a special role.

celebration.headline: You met the neighbours.
celebration.keepsake: Legs were counted. Wings were found. Every creature went home again.

title: A5 Leaf Collage
description: Objective: create art with nature, taking influence from what the children see around them.
activity: Collect leaves outside, then glue them into patterns and pictures on A5 paper.
preparation: Glue sticks and A5 paper in a bag. One sheet per child, plus a few spares.
space_needed: Anywhere with fallen leaves, and a dry spot to sit and stick.

steps.name: Collect
steps.note: Ask children to gather fallen leaves and petals from the ground — ones that have already fallen.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Let's go outside to collect leaves and petals from the ground, in a variety of shades and colours.
prompts: Let's go outside to collect leaves and petals from the ground, in a variety of shades and colours.

steps.name: Create
steps.note: Gather the children back inside. Let them take their time with this.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Take a seat. Using the materials you collected, create a collage of something you saw in nature.
prompts: Take a seat. Using the materials you collected, create a collage of something you saw in nature.

steps.name: Glue
steps.note: Give the class ideas, drawing on what they saw in nature.
steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: You can cut and stick pieces of leaves into different patterns or shapes.
prompts: You can cut and stick pieces of leaves into different patterns or shapes.
Perhaps you want to make an insect, a flower, or a landscape?

steps.name: Present
steps.note: Ask if anyone wants to show their art to the rest of the class.
steps.label: Say to your class
prompts: How did you use your natural materials to create different parts of your piece?
What inspired you in nature to make this?

closing_prompts.question: Show your collage to a partner. What can they see in it?

closing_prompts.note: Shape, colour, size, smell. Descriptive language lives here.
closing_prompts.question: Which leaf was your favourite, and where did it come from?

closing_prompts.note: Back to the earth. Nothing in nature is wasted.
closing_prompts.question: What will happen to the leaves we did not use?

primer.why: Making art with found nature asks children to look twice: once at the leaf, once at the world. The picture is theirs; the materials belong to the place.
primer.summary: Children collect leaves outside and glue them into patterns and pictures on A5 paper, taking influence from what they can see around them.

celebration.headline: Art, straight from the ground.
celebration.keepsake: Leaves became trees, clouds, birds and insects. Made entirely of this place.
celebration.nextWeekTease: Next week: our Earth's magnificent trees.

title: Our Earth's Magnificent Trees
prompt: Why are trees so important for our existence?
description: Objective: understand why trees matter for our existence (humans) and for the other creatures on our planet.
activity: Walk among your trees, talk about why they matter, and end by thanking one.
preparation: Nothing to bring. If it has rained, bark is darker and smells stronger: even better.
space_needed: Anywhere you can see trees, even over a fence. One tree you can reach for the closing.

steps.name: Walk
steps.note: Bark, leaves, height, shape. How many different trees can the class spot?

tips.then: Touch two different barks. Smooth or rough? Same or different?
tips.when: If they say all trees look the same...

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Walk around your outside space, taking note of all the different trees you can see.

steps.name: Discuss
steps.note: Prompt children to discuss amongst themselves. They produce the air we need to breathe (oxygen).

tips.then: Hold your breath for three seconds together. Where does the next breath come from? Trees made part of it.

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: Why are trees so important for our existence (humans)?

steps.name: Creatures
steps.note: e.g. birds for homes and food (nuts & fruit), insects.

tips.then: Look closer: who is walking on the trunk? Who is under the bark?

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: What other creatures on our planet need trees to live?

steps.name: Imagine
steps.note: Sit with the question. Let the silence do some of the teaching.

tips.then: That worry is care. Tell them: that is exactly why we look after trees.

steps.label: Say to your class
steps.prompt: If there were no trees on our planet, would we be alive?

closing_prompts.question: Ask all children to hug and thank the tree.
What did the bark feel like?

closing_prompts.note: Some children will whisper it to themselves. That counts.
closing_prompts.question: What would you say to this tree if it could hear you?

primer.why: A child who has thanked a tree treats trees differently. This session turns the biggest living things on the school grounds from scenery into neighbours.
primer.summary: Children walk among the trees of their outside space and talk about why trees matter: for the air we breathe and for the creatures that live in and around them.

celebration.headline: You thanked the trees.
celebration.keepsake: The air we breathe, the homes above us. Today the class said thank you.
